name: legba
desc: Multiprotocol credentials bruteforcer/password sprayer and enumerator
why: A multiprotocol credential sprayer is a sharp lens on how many auth protocols quietly exist, though it leans toward offensive tooling.

brief.what_it_is: Legba is a command-line credential bruteforcer and password sprayer, with an enumerator component, written in Rust on the Tokio async runtime. The README's example takes a target host, a username, and a password wordlist file, then runs `legba smb --target domain.local --username administrator --password wordlist.txt`. It supports many protocols (HTTP, DNS, SSH, FTP, SMTP, RDP, VNC, SQL, NoSQL, LDAP, Kerberos, SAMBA, SNMP, STOMP, MQTT, and more). Results are exported in several output formats. The README also describes a REST API and an MCP server for driving it programmatically.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it was built to get better performance and stability while using fewer resources than similar tools, citing a benchmark page. It is framed as a multiprotocol replacement for single-protocol brute-force tools.
brief.how_it_works: Credentials come from wordlist files, ranges, permutations, or expression generators. Requests run concurrently through a Tokio async architecture with configurable workers, and rate control covers limits, delays, jitter, and retries. Scan state can be saved and restored to resume interrupted runs. YAML 'recipes' describe more complex authentication flows.

commands_seen.context: Adds the project's custom Homebrew tap from the GitHub repo; this is the Homebrew route the README gives.
Installs legba from that tap after the tap is added.
Quick-start example: sprays the SMB protocol at domain.local as administrator, using wordlist.txt for passwords.
Optional: installs a legba skill for AI coding agents so they know the syntax, plugins, recipes, and API.
Installs cargo-license, which the README suggests for listing dependency licenses.
Run after installing cargo-license to view licenses of the project's dependencies.

brief.install_notes: The README offers precompiled binaries on the GitHub latest-release page, or the Homebrew tap above. Building from source is not described in the README I read. The README says there are no native dependencies. No account, API key, or runtime is mentioned for basic use. The REST API, MCP server, recipes, and protocol plugins are documented on the docs site, which I did not read beyond the homepage.
brief.standout: Most credential sprayers cover one protocol. This one covers a long list in a single Rust binary, and it ships a REST API, an MCP server, and an AI-agent skill, which is unusual for offensive tooling of this kind. Its stated pitch is resource use and throughput against similar tools.
brief.status: unknown. The docs site and GitHub repo are live, the README has a CI badge, a release badge, a Discord link, and a contributors graph, and the repo is public. I did not see a last-release date or last-commit date in what I fetched, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: Licensed GPL-3.0. It is offensive-security tooling built for password spraying and brute forcing; the README has no explicit legal or authorization warning. Use against systems you do not own or have no permission to test is illegal in most places. Cross-platform claims come from the README and are unverified. The Homebrew route requires adding a third-party tap by URL. I read only the homepage and README, not the usage, recipe, or per-protocol docs, so the full option list is unchecked. The scout note's 'offensive tooling' lean is accurate.
quotes: Legba is a multiprotocol credentials bruteforcer / password sprayer and enumerator built with Rust and the Tokio asynchronous runtime in order to achieve better performances and stability while consuming less resources than similar tools
100% Rust - Legba is entirely written in Rust, does not have native dependencies and can be easily compiled for all operating systems and architectures.
Smart Session Management - Save and restore session state to resume interrupted scans.
